name: Sara Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not connected to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you tell me a little about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Sara, I'm 27, and I'm engaged to Daniel, we're getting married next September at our church. He drives a delivery van for a parcel company. We rent a small flat on Victoria Street, near my mum and my two aunties. I work at Goldcrust, the big bread bakery by the river, nearly a year now.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the slicer and bagger at the end of Line 1. The loaves come out of the cooling spiral, go through the slicer blades, and the bagger puffs open a bag and pushes the loaf in, and I tie them off and watch for jams. I'm still not quick at changing the blades, Mr. Hughes the supervisor stands over me for that, and I've cut my glove twice. I like the smell, and I like that what I make ends up on people's tables, it's honest work. I'm on earlies, so I'm in bed by nine, which Daniel teases me about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, people get carried away with gadgets. I don't use any of it myself, I don't need a computer to tell me how to tie a bag. At church I'd probably just say thank God, and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things go on as they are, and that suits me. I've got a wedding to pay for and I need the job steady. I'd rather nothing changed at all, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts, try to get quicker at the blade changes so Mr. Hughes leaves me alone. Daniel and I are putting fifty a week into a jar for the wedding, which is everything we can spare. I'd keep doing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful. Like a normal Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything new at Goldcrust already, any machines coming in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a robot that stacks the trays on Line 2, they put it in last year. Two ladies went off that job, one retired and one moved to the packing room. Nobody made a fuss, it was done decently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the wedding money if something goes wrong, like the car or the rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the jar pays for it and the wedding gets smaller. It's happened once already, the van needed tyres. My mum says the wedding is the vows, not the cake, and she's right, but I'd still like a nice cake.

S0.say: She'd say she isn't surprised because people get carried away with gadgets, and that she doesn't need a computer to tie a bag. At church she'd just say thank God.
S0.think: She thinks it means things carry on, which suits her because she has a wedding to pay for and needs a steady job. She'd rather nothing changed at all.
S0.do: Keeps working her shifts and tries to get faster at blade changes. Continues putting fifty a week into a jar for the wedding, which is all she and her fiancé can spare.
S0.quote: My mum says the wedding is the vows, not the cake, and she's right, but I'd still like a nice cake.
S0.fieldNote: Sara's world centres on her wedding, her church and her family nearby. She's happy for nothing to change and has never used AI. She judged the tray-stacking robot as fair because it was handled decently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people will just have to work hard and adapt, same as always. My grandad came to this country with nothing and worked two jobs. I wouldn't be one to complain or ask for handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be frightened. My job is exactly the kind of thing a machine can do, it's watching and tying and clearing jams. I'm not good with new technology, I only got a smartphone two years ago, so if they want people who can work computers, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work as hard as I can and never be late, so if they're choosing who stays, they choose me. We'd cut back, no takeaways, no new clothes, and probably make the wedding smaller, maybe just the church and a lunch in the hall. I wouldn't go on any course, I'd ask Mr. Hughes if there's another job in the bakery I could move to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, all the time. Like a stone in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't ask for handouts. What if the job did go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my family first. My uncle runs a small cleaning company, he'd find me something. And the church would help, they always do. Government money would be the last thing, I'd feel ashamed taking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you talk to Daniel about making the wedding smaller?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talk, yes. He'd say it doesn't matter to him. But I'd feel it, because I've been picturing that day since I was a girl, and I'd feel like the machines took that from me too.

S1.say: She'd say people must work hard and adapt as always, pointing to her grandfather who arrived with nothing and worked two jobs. She wouldn't complain or ask for handouts.
S1.think: Privately she'd be frightened, because watching, tying and clearing jams is exactly what machines can do. She's not good with technology and doubts she'd fit a computer-heavy job.
S1.do: Works as hard as possible and is never late so she's chosen to stay. Cuts takeaways and new clothes, shrinks the wedding to a church service and a hall lunch, and asks her supervisor about other jobs in the bakery rather than taking a course.
S1.feel: Constant worry, like a stone in her stomach.
S1.quote: I've been picturing that day since I was a girl, and I'd feel like the machines took that from me too.
S1.fieldNote: Her public answer is about hard work and self-reliance; privately she's frightened and knows she's poorly placed for technical work. Her safety net is family and church, with government money a shameful last resort. The wedding is where the loss would hit her most personally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who built this have a lot to answer for. Rushing things like that, without a thought for ordinary families. I'd say we'll pray and get through it, because that's what you do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be finished at Goldcrust within the year. If a robot can tie the bags and change the blades and do Mr. Hughes's job too, what's left for me? And Daniel's job is driving, and they'd have vans that drive themselves, so both of us at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the wedding savings and use them to live on, and we'd put the wedding off, which breaks my heart. We'd give up the flat and move into my mum's back room, she's offered before. I'd go to my uncle about cleaning work and to the church about anything going, even unpaid, just to be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground's been pulled away. I think I'd cry a lot, and I don't cry easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said both of you at once. What would that night look like, when you both knew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sit in the flat with the TV off. Daniel would go quiet, he always does, and I'd make tea nobody drinks. Then we'd pray, because I wouldn't know what else to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said government money would be the last thing. In this picture, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there was nothing else, yes, I suppose I'd have to. I'd hate it. But if everybody's out of work at once, it's not really a handout, is it, it's not anyone's fault.

S2.say: She'd say the people who built this have a lot to answer for for rushing without thought for ordinary families. She'd say they'd pray and get through it.
S2.think: She expects to lose her job within the year and fears her fiancé's driving job would go at the same time. She sees nothing left for her if robots can do the whole line.
S2.do: Stops wedding savings and lives on them, postpones the wedding and moves with her fiancé into her mother's back room. Asks her uncle for cleaning work and the church for anything going, even unpaid.
S2.feel: Like the ground pulled away, crying a lot though she rarely does.
S2.quote: Daniel would go quiet, he always does, and I'd make tea nobody drinks. Then we'd pray, because I wouldn't know what else to do.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture hits her household twice, since both she and her fiancé do automatable work. Her firm stance against government money softens when she sees mass job loss as nobody's fault. Faith and family are her only real plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at least we'd have warning, so families can get ready. People should save and look after each other. I'd say the companies ought to give people time and treat them decently, like with the tray robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 32, and I think I'd lose the job, just later. We'd be married by then, which matters to me. It's a few more years to be ready, but I don't think I'd be any better at computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd get married next September as planned, but small, and put whatever's left into savings instead. I'd try to save a little each week after that, maybe twenty-five. I'd ask Mr. Hughes to train me on more jobs in the bakery, so I'm the last one they let go, not the first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I could sleep. It'd feel like a long storm warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about children differently in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. We want children, two or three. But I wouldn't want to bring a baby into a house with no job coming in. We might wait, and that makes me sad, because I don't want to be an old mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't be any better at computers. Would you try, with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, if Daniel helped me. But I've tried before, with the online banking, and I end up getting him to do it. I'd rather spend the time learning more about the bakery, real work I can see.

S3.say: She'd say at least there's warning so families can prepare, save and look after each other. Companies, she'd say, should give time and treat people decently.
S3.think: She expects to lose her job later rather than sooner, but takes comfort that she'd be married by then. She doesn't think five years would make her any better with computers.
S3.do: Marries next September as planned but on a small scale, saving what's left, then saves about twenty-five a week. Asks her supervisor to train her on more bakery jobs so she's the last let go.
S3.feel: Worried but able to sleep, like a long storm warning.
S3.quote: I wouldn't want to bring a baby into a house with no job coming in.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her keep the wedding, which clearly matters most, but pushes back children. She'd learn more of the bakery rather than computers, staying with what she can see and touch. She still expects to lose the job, so the threat remains real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and families should use it, save, and help their young ones get a trade. I wouldn't be one to panic. Things work out if you work hard and keep faith.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37, married, maybe with a little one. I think I'd still lose the job in the end, but ten years is a lot of wages. The hard part would be if it landed just when we had small children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Goldcrust as long as they'll have me and learn every job on the line. We'd save steadily, maybe fifty a week once the wedding's paid for. I'd wait and see what happens before I made any big changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back, but mostly I'd get on with life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned helping young ones get a trade. Which trades would you think are safe in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. I'd have said plumbing or nursing, but if robots can do hands-on work too, maybe nothing's safe. I'd still want my children to know how to work hard, whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said things work out if you work hard. Do you believe that, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to. Maybe I believe it less than I say it. But I'd rather believe that than sit around waiting for somebody to save us.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is a long time for families to save and help their young ones learn a trade, and that she wouldn't panic. Things work out with hard work and faith.
S4.think: She expects to lose the job eventually but values ten more years of wages. Her worry is it landing just when they have small children.
S4.do: Keeps working at the bakery as long as possible and learns every job on the line. Saves about fifty a week once the wedding is paid for and waits before making any big changes.
S4.feel: Mostly gets on with life, with unease in the background.
S4.quote: Maybe I believe it less than I say it. But I'd rather believe that than sit around waiting for somebody to save us.
S4.fieldNote: Even with ten years, she doesn't plan to retrain and admits she doesn't know which trades would be safe. She half admits her faith in hard work is stronger in public than in private. The timing against her plans for children is what keeps her worried.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because it would take Daniel's job and mine together, before the wedding. What would help is the companies keeping people on longer and treating them decently, and help for families from the church and the community. I'd want work, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of people at the bakery go to church or mosque or temple. When the work goes, that's where people will turn, and those places need to be ready too.

headlineQuote: I don't need a computer to tell me how to tie a bag.
portrait: Sara Mensah is a 27-year-old slicer and bagger operator at a big bread bakery, engaged to a delivery driver and saving fifty a week for a church wedding. She's never used AI, finds technology hard and wants nothing to change. Steady change frightens her privately even as she talks publicly about hard work and no handouts; fast AGI, which could take both her job and her fiancé's at once, leaves her panicked and ready to postpone the wedding. With more time she keeps the wedding but puts off children, and learns more bakery jobs rather than computers. Family and church are her safety net, and she admits her faith in hard work is stronger said aloud than felt.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would take both her job and her fiancé's together, before the wedding.
whatWouldHelp: Companies keeping people on longer and treating them decently, plus support for families from church and community; she wants work, not handouts.
